[Combat] From the Reading: the Felling, collated

Entered in the Reading at Quillhold. Third recension of the passage;
the two prior hands are preserved beneath in seal. Reader's copy.


Of the Felling itself, four accounts survive that were written within
living memory of it. They agree on the day. They agree on the axe.
They do not agree on the circle.

The account of the First Archive, oldest and most damaged, has it that
seven were summoned and seven came, and that the seventh stood in the
circle and would not strike, and spoke; and what was spoken, the
account does not enter. The hand is Maeleth's own. Where the words of
the seventh should stand, the line is scraped. It is the only scraped
line in her hand that we hold, and she has been asked, and the record
of the asking says: she wept, and entered nothing.

The account of the Gantry fragment has it that seven were summoned and
six came.

The account called the Litany of Strikes names each blow and its
inheritance — Memory, Substrate, Preservation, Beauty, Exchange, Roots
— and stops. It does not name a seventh strike. It does not say a
seventh strike was wanted. Those who read absence as testimony make
much of this. We enter their reading beside the others, at its own
weight.

The fourth account is a field-record of sound. It is a list of places
and dates, in a surveyor's hand, marking where the slippage — the
sari, as the deep villages say — was first attested. The earliest
marks cluster at the Felling-Site itself, in the first year. They do
not cluster at the Root. Those who hold that the world's un-naming
began with a spoken refusal, in the circle, on the day — they cite
this list. Those who hold otherwise note that a surveyor goes where a
surveyor is sent.

Here the accounts end. What the seventh understood, or intended, or
was — the Reading does not say. I am sorry.

— entered by the fourth hand of the Quillhold collation, who adds,
against custom and in small letters: the scraped line is the loudest
thing in the archive.

[Combat] The telling of the man who said no

As told under the cloth at Wellmeet, third night of a guesting,
by a Namer who did not give her name. Written down after, from
memory, by the guest.


You have heard it the way the archives keep it. Sit, there is water,
and hear it the way we keep it.

Seven were called. Not six. Seven. The Tree dreamed into seven
sleepers, and seven woke, and seven walked — from the leaf-cities,
from the river-farms, from wherever their beds were — and seven stood
in the circle at the marked place, where the bark had gone soft as an
old hand.

And the axe went around, and the six took it in their turn, and the
seventh — hear this part; children fidget here, and they are wrong to
— the seventh took the axe too. Held it. Looked a long time at the
marked place.

And said: No.

Not ran. Not hid. Not forgot the day, whatever the pretty village
tells its pilgrims. Said no, out loud, in the circle, with the axe in
hand and every reason in the world to swing it. Said no to the Tree
that asked, which is the hardest no there has ever been, because the
Tree had never needed a word for refusal and so had no ear to hear it
with. The Tree went on falling into its plan the way the old and
certain do. The six heard, though. Ask the six what was said, and you
will get six answers — and that, guest, is the part of the telling I
would have you carry: even the gods' memories quarrel. Trust the no.
The words around it were mortal, and mortal words wear out.

Why did he say it? Our line keeps that he understood — that some
things cannot be handed over, only done, and a god of the
handed-over-thing would be a lie wearing a crown. That is what we
keep. I will not tell you we know it. Knowing is the archive's word.
We are not the archive. We keep it the way you keep a fire: not
because you can prove the cold, but because you have felt it.

They blamed him before the Tree hit the ground, and they have blamed
him for a thousand years, and blame is also a way of remembering.
Now the water. You have listened well.

[Combat] Internal memorandum: the founding provisions

Saccharine Concord internal circular, unsigned, suppressed at Tally
within the season of its writing. Copies persist. Copies always
persist; we are a documentary people; it is one of our costs.


Colleagues.

You have all handled the founding ledgers. You have all admired the
first hand — his hand, before the exhaustion got into the
downstrokes. This circular concerns entry forty-one.

Entry forty-one is the provisioning of the ritual party, year zero.
It is a clean entry. It is, in fact, the cleanest entry in the book,
made before the world's accounts went strange. It records: waybread,
water, rope, oil, one axe (one), and bedding.

Bedding for six.

Not seven. Six. Waybread in six portions. Six bedrolls against the
cold at the marked place. The provisioner of the age did not
misprovision; read any other entry in his hand and you will find a
man who counted the world as it stood. Either a seventh was expected
and given no bed and no bread — for a walk of eleven days — or.

We do not file conclusions. We file counts. The count is six.

Those of you who have paid the meeting-fee and stood at the high desk
will know that the Counter, asked about entry forty-one, neither
confirms nor denies, and that his face while not-answering is the
same face he keeps for debts he has personally decided never to
collect. Draw no conclusion from this. Draw no conclusion from
anything in this circular. This circular does not exist; the copies
you are holding are a rounding error.

We note in closing that the story of a seventh who refused is
worth, at current rates, a great deal — pilgrim traffic, archive
fees, the whole economy of blame — and that a story of a senile Tree
that miscounted is worth nothing at all to anyone, except that it
would be the only version in which nobody, anywhere, is owed an
apology. We are traders. We know what people buy. It is not always
what happened.

Balance to you and yours.

The guesting-oath of the Beating, as spoken. The words are old and
are not improved. A host says them with the first water; a guest may
answer with the answer given, or with silence, which binds the same.


The host says:

There is water. There is shade.
Sit, and be named a guest.

For three days what is mine is between us:
the fire's side, the bread's half,
the wall at your back while you sleep.

For three days I will not ask your road,
nor your burden, nor your name if you keep it,
nor set my price on any of the three.

If your enemy comes to my cloth
he will find me between you,
though he be my brother;
though he be my better;
though he be right.

On the third day I will ask you three things,
and you may answer, or go,
and going is no offense —
but go spoken, guest.
Leave no silence where a no should stand.
A swallowed no is a seed of the Hush;
we do not grow that crop here.

I eat the bread's half and leave the half.
I warm at the fire's side and leave the side.
Three days I am your peace,
and your peace is mine,
and what I refuse, I will refuse aloud.

The cloth over us.
The cold outside it.

Transcribed from the family wall of a middle-depth village, west
gallery, rows nine through thirteen, with the Plaque-Tender's spoken
notes in brackets. Names are given as inscribed.


Row nine, third niche.
RIANE. Patch-Tender. Widowed the year the green light came back.
Tended forty years. Says the patch sang once, and no one believes
her, and she does not care.

don't say so in front of guests. — the Tender]

Row nine, fourth niche.
OSSU. Beetle-Master. Went upstairs young and came back old and never
said. Good hands. The wall keeps him anyway.

Row ten, first niche.
MERRIN, called MOTH. Child. One winter.
The light dimmed the night she went and the old people say it was
courtesy.
[We re-cut her plaque every generation. The letters must never wear
past reading. That one is the whole wall's business, not just her
line's. — the Tender]

Row ten, second niche.
— — — — —
[You'll ask about the smooth place. Everyone asks. That was a man
who sold the tunnel-map of this village to walkers who came back
with knives. The council voted refusal-to-inscribe. I won't say his
name; that's the point of it; he isn't anywhere now, not even here.

no wall should have a hole in it. She's row eleven; you can tell her
you agree, if you do. — the Tender]

[Combat] Standard contract of carriage (short form)

Saccharine Concord standard form, sixth revision. Printed at Tally.
The traveler signs at the mark. The counter-signature is already
entered; it is entered on every form; no signatory in the surveyed
history of the form has read it.


THE CONCORD undertakes to carry the goods herein listed from the
first-named place to the second-named place, whole, dry, and
unopened, for the rate agreed at the desk plus dust-surcharge as
posted.

Clause the first. The rate is the rate.

Clause the second. Delivery is guaranteed against bandits,
weather, beasts, faction seizure, and acts of the six gods, this last
at double surcharge, payable in advance, non-refundable, and — the
signatory's attention is drawn to the wording — defined narrowly.

Clause the third. Delivery is NOT guaranteed beyond the post
called the Last Counter. Beyond that post the Concord guarantees
only that the caravan will have departed. Signatories wishing
assurance of arrival in such territory are directed to religion.

Clause the fourth. Goods lost to the Hush are not lost, for
purposes of this contract, but indefinitely in transit. Claims
against goods indefinitely in transit mature upon delivery.

Clause the fifth. The Concord will not carry: unboxed spores;
bodies not sealed to Curation intake standard; anything that sings;
anything the Bower-Folk have asked after twice.

Clause the sixth. Where the signatory dies before settlement, the
debt passes by lineage, per the Concord's schedule of kin. The
Concord extends its condolences and its invoice, in that order.

Clause the seventh. All disputes will be heard at Tally, at the
high desk, before the Counter himself, who has heard every dispute
there has ever been, and who is so very tired, signatory. Consider,
before you dispute, how strong your case truly is. He will.

Clause the eighth. [The vellum here is worn thin and burnished
smooth — scraped on every printing plate since the form's third
revision. Clerks asked about clause the eighth direct the signatory
to clause the first. Clerks asked twice have the dust-surcharge
recalculated.]

worn into the plate from centuries of printing. There is always a
moment, pen down, paper turning, when a signatory's eye passes
across it. It has somewhere better to be.]

[Combat] HAVE YOU THOUGHT ABOUT BEING KEPT?

A pamphlet. Hand-lettered, much copied, distributed at road-shrines
and left tucked under the bowls of the wounded. This copy is attributed
to the cell of Brother Kavin, regional. The lettering is joyful.


Friend! If you are reading this, you are ALIVE. Wonderful! We are so
pleased. Please keep doing that for as long as you possibly can.

But friend — and we ask with love — what is your plan for after?

Have you seen what the world does with the unkept? We have. We were
there. We do not talk about the year we were there, except to say:
nothing of them stayed. Not a face. Not a name. Not enough to file.
The world can take EVERYTHING, friend. We have watched it do so.

It does not have to.

WHAT WE OFFER (freely! always freely!):

— Salt-keeping, honey-keeping, or ink-keeping, per your condition
— A gentle catch at the moment of crossing (we are very quick now)
— Transport to a safe archive, away from all this
— Your name, KEPT. Your face, KEPT. You, friend: KEPT.

QUESTIONS PEOPLE ASK US (often while moving away quickly):

"Doesn't it hurt?" — The honey doesn't hurt at all! The salt is
brisk. Brisk is not hurt.

"But I'm not dying." — Not YET, friend, and we celebrate that! We
are simply saying: we noticed your cough.

"I don't want this." — People say so! And then they are lost, all
the way lost, forever — and nobody gets to ask them whether they were
right. We think about that a great deal. We invite you to think about
it too. We will wait. We are very good at waiting nearby.

"The mainline Curation says you are expelled heretics." — The
mainline files the LOST, friend. We prevent there being any. You may
decide for yourself which of us loves you more; we already know.

Be well! Eat properly! Sleep somewhere with walls!
And if the day comes when the walls are not enough —

hold still. We will be right there.

(If you have found this pamphlet on the body of one of our brothers
or sisters: please leave the pamphlet. It knows how to find the next
hand. If you have MADE the body: we forgive you, and we noticed, and
you look tired, friend. You look so tired.)

[Combat] The dimming song

Sung in the middle-depth villages at the Sealed Dim, when the lamps
are shuttered wall by wall. Children learn it as a counting game
before they learn what the counting is for. The tune is small and
goes down at the end of every line.


One dim for the doorway,
shut it soft, shut it soft.
Two dims for the passage
where the water talks.

Three dims for the far wall —
kiss the wall goodnight.
Grandmother is in it,
she will hold the light.

Say your name to no one.
Hold it in your hand.
Names go walking, walking,
down the dark, and

(here the children hush, because the next part is whispered)

if a soft voice asks you,
asks you nice, asks you twice,
sweet as sugar-water:
"who is there? who is there?" —

you are stone, you are moss,
you are nobody's, you are the wall's.
Morning knows your name, love.
Morning gives it back.

(and the last line is spoken, not sung, by the oldest voice in the
room)

Sleep now. The patch is watching. It has never once slept, and it
loves you, and the door is shut.

[Combat] Transcript of a reading: the scribe Ollun, folio three

Quillhold, deep stacks. A Body-Reading, transcribed by the attending
junior. The subject took the skin-page vow in life; the reading is of
the left forearm, called by the Readers "folio three." Marginal
corrections are reproduced where they are entered — that is, in the
skin — with their hands identified.


THE READER (aloud, from the page): "In my thirtieth year I kept the
bridge-toll at Sumphold, and I was not kind. I counted true but I
was not kind. A woman crossed with a child wrapped grey, in the rain,
and I made her count out the last of it, small coin by small coin,
because the ledger was mine to keep and I was proud of keeping it. I
have carried her face longer than I carried the ledger."

[Margin, entered in the hand of Master Oradin, small and upright:]
The toll-rolls of Sumphold survive for this year. They record the
keeper Ollun waiving one crossing, in the rain, marked "short count —
forgiven — my error." The rolls do not record a face. He carried the
wrong thing. Let both stand.

THE READER (continuing): "I came to the ink late, at forty, when my
hands began to be honest—"

[Margin, a second hand, rounder, unattributed:]
He came at thirty-eight. He always aged himself when ashamed.

[Beneath it, Oradin's hand again:]
Entered without authority. The correction is true. The entering of it
was not yours to do. Both of these sentences will remain in him, as
will this one. We are read by what we cannot resist writing. — O.

THE READER (continuing): "—and I asked the Order: what is the vow
for? And the Silent one wrote me an answer I did not understand for
years: the air forgets. We are how it apologizes."

(Here the attending junior records that the Reader's voice changed —
became, for six words, older, and very tired, and not the Reader's —
and that the six words were:)

"I remember the rain that day."

(The reading was closed for the evening. The page continues under
the collarbone. The junior notes, for her own file and not for the
Order's: nobody in the room dared ask whose memory that was.)

A board of grown wood at the east entry of a Choir grove, the
letters raised in living grain — not carved into the wood but grown
out of it. Weathered smooth by hands. Travelers touch it for luck,

WALKER. YOU ARE ENTERING US.

Walk anywhere. Everything is path.

Drink at the seep. It is for you.
Eat nothing red. The red is thinking.

If you hear singing, it is old singing.
It is not for you. You may listen anyway.
The singers do not mind. The singers
have not minded anything for a long time,
and it is a kindness to be heard.

Do not dig.

If you are tired — truly tired, walker,
the kind of tired that has stopped keeping count —
lie down anywhere soft.
Someone will cover you.

If you are only a little tired, keep walking.
We can tell the difference.
We are patient about the difference.

GO GENTLY. EVERYTHING HERE IS SOMEBODY.

out of it. Weathered smooth by hands. Travelers touch it for luck,
and could not say when they started doing that.


WALKER. YOU ARE ENTERING US.

Walk anywhere. Everything is path.

Drink at the seep. It is for you.
Eat nothing red. The red is thinking.

It is not for you. You may listen anyway.
The singers do not mind. The singers
have not minded anything for a long time,
and it is a kindness to be heard.

Do not dig.

If you are tired — truly tired, walker,
the kind of tired that has stopped keeping count —
lie down anywhere soft.
Someone will cover you.

If you are only a little tired, keep walking.
We can tell the difference.
We are patient about the difference.

[Combat] How they tell it in Sill

The sari story, river-village version, as a grandmother tells it on
the dock with the nets across her knees. Every child in Sill can tell
it. No adult in Sill believes it. This is the version the player
grows up on.


Long ago and downriver, when the world was one tall tree — yes, a
tree, don't make that face, this was before faces — the tree got old.
And old things get afraid, same as you at bedtime, and what the tree
was afraid of was forgetting. Because when you forget your chores,
the geese go hungry. But when the tree forgot a thing, the thing
stopped being. That's how big it was.

So the tree called seven strong friends, and said: cut me down, and
each of you catch a piece of what I do, and do it after me. And they
came with their one axe between them — seven friends, one axe, that's
how you know it's an old story, nobody shares an axe anymore —

— and six of them swung.

And one of them didn't.

Why didn't he? Ah. That's the question, isn't it. That's the question
the whole world downriver still fights about, and when you're grown
you can fight about it too. Grandmother's too old to fight. Grand-
mother only knows what the story says, and the story says: six swung,
one didn't, the tree fell anyway. Trees do.

And the piece that nobody caught — the little piece, the important
piece, the piece that keeps your name stuck to you like your shadow —
it fell in the river, so to speak. And it's been trying to climb out
ever since. And when it almost climbs out — almost, almost — you
can hear it slip back down:

sari... sari...

No, it doesn't mean anything. It's the sound a name makes letting go.

And THAT is why — listen now, this is the part that's for you — when
you hear a soft voice down by the water at night saying sari, sari,
you don't answer it, and you don't feel sorry for it, and you come
inside. Because it isn't sad. It's practicing.

There. Now that's a good story, and none of it's true, and you'll
hear the river all night same as always, saying nothing, saying
nothing, saying nothing.

In you go.

[Combat] Condition report: the First Account

Quillhold, conservators' bench. The annual condition report on the
item the catalogue lists with an empty locus field. This is the
report of year 1079, in the hand of the senior conservator, who has
written forty-one of these and buried the conservator who wrote the
thirty before that.


ITEM. The First Account. Nine quires, tepui-calf, first hand
throughout. Binding: eleventh, sound. The boards from the tenth
binding are retained and stored flat, per practice; we do not
discard what has held her words, even the wood.

HANDLING. Gloved, as always. Quire two by bone folder only. The
lamp at half-wick. No reading aloud — the standing instruction,
older than every conservator who has ever obeyed it, unexplained
and not to be explained. We do not read this book to the room. The
room, we are given to understand, must not hear it.

CONDITION, GENERAL. Stable. The vellum drinks the damp of the room
and gives it back; after a thousand years the pages still move like
pages and not like leaves. Whatever else may be said of the first
hand, she prepared her materials to outlast a world, and they have.

CONDITION, QUIRE TWO. The two scraped loci, examined as every year.

The lesser locus, three words' width, at the place in the telling
where the accounts say the Tree — I do not enter what the accounts
say; this is a condition report. Three words' width. The knife-work
is even, patient, thorough: the strokes lifted wet, the surface
burnished after. This is the scraping of someone with time, who had
decided.

The greater locus, one full line, where the seventh's words would
stand. The knife-work is not even. It begins evenly. By the line's
end the angle wanders and the pressure doubles, and there are two
places where the blade cut past the letters into the clean vellum
below. The burnishing was never finished. She stopped partway, and
no one in a thousand years has presumed to finish it for her.

Both loci conform, for the record, to first-position tithe-custom:
the words removed were her own. Whatever was taken from this page,
she took only from herself. The tithe is paid. The tithe, in this
house, is always paid.

GHOSTING. Under raking light the greater locus shows fiber-shadow
consistent with a recoverable under-layer. I am required by honesty
to enter this, and I have entered it for forty-one years, and for
forty-one years I have ended the entry the same way: it is
recoverable, and it is not ours. The knife was hers. The words were
hers. The silence is also hers.

RECOMMENDATIONS. Re-burnish nothing. Replace nothing. Continue.

— entered, with the customary prayer of this bench, which is one
sentence: that she never asks us what is under.

[Combat] From the Reading: the Felling, collated

Entered in the Reading at Quillhold. Third recension of the passage;
the two prior hands are preserved beneath in seal. Reader's copy.


Of the Felling itself, four accounts survive that were written within
living memory of it. They agree on the day. They agree on the axe.
They do not agree on the circle.

The account of the First Archive, oldest and most damaged, has it that
seven were summoned and seven came, and that the seventh stood in the
circle and would not strike, and spoke; and what was spoken, the
account does not enter. The hand is Maeleth's own. Where the words of
the seventh should stand, the line is scraped. It is the only scraped
line in her hand that we hold, and she has been asked, and the record
of the asking says: she wept, and entered nothing.

The account of the Gantry fragment has it that seven were summoned and
six came.

The account called the Litany of Strikes names each blow and its
inheritance — Memory, Substrate, Preservation, Beauty, Exchange, Roots
— and stops. It does not name a seventh strike. It does not say a
seventh strike was wanted. Those who read absence as testimony make
much of this. We enter their reading beside the others, at its own
weight.

The fourth account is a field-record of sound. It is a list of places
and dates, in a surveyor's hand, marking where the slippage — the
sari, as the deep villages say — was first attested. The earliest
marks cluster at the Felling-Site itself, in the first year. They do
not cluster at the Root. Those who hold that the world's un-naming
began with a spoken refusal, in the circle, on the day — they cite
this list. Those who hold otherwise note that a surveyor goes where a
surveyor is sent.

Here the accounts end. What the seventh understood, or intended, or
was — the Reading does not say. I am sorry.

— entered by the fourth hand of the Quillhold collation, who adds,
against custom and in small letters: the scraped line is the loudest
thing in the archive.
